title: Monasteries of Darjeeling and Ghoom: A Visitor's Guide
meta_description: Yiga Choeling at Ghoom, Samten Choling, Bhutia Busty, Mahakal on Observatory Hill and the Tibetan Refugee Centre: history, fees, timings and etiquette.
summary: Darjeeling's best-known monastery is Yiga Choeling at Ghoom, founded in 1850, with a 15 ft statue of the future Buddha. Pair it with Samten Choling and the Sakya monastery nearby, then Bhutia Busty, the shared Mahakal shrine on Observatory Hill and the Tibetan Refugee Self Help Centre. Go early, walk clockwise and ask before photographs.

sections.heading: Why Buddhism runs deep in these hills
paras: Darjeeling's very name points to Buddhism. It is usually read as dorje, the thunderbolt sceptre used in Tibetan ritual, and ling, a place: the place of the thunderbolt. Tradition links it to a Buddhist shrine called Dorje-ling that once stood on Observatory Hill, the knoll above Chowrasta, before the British hill station was built. The Chogyal of Sikkim granted the hill tract to the East India Company in 1835, and Lepcha, Bhutia, Sherpa and Tibetan families kept their monasteries going through the tea and railway years that followed.

A second wave came after 1959, when Tibetans who fled with and after the Dalai Lama settled in Darjeeling. Today you will find monasteries of more than one Tibetan Buddhist school within a short ride of each other, Hindu and Buddhist worship on the same hilltop, and prayer flags on almost every ridge. None of the sites below needs more than a small fee or a donation, and most are best seen in the quiet of the morning.

sections.heading: Yiga Choeling, the old monastery at Ghoom
paras: Yiga Choeling, the monastery everyone calls Ghoom Monastery, was founded in 1850 by Lama Sherab Gyatso and belongs to the Gelug school, the tradition of the Dalai Lama. It stands a short walk below the main road at Ghoom, about 7–8 km from Darjeeling and close to the highest station on the toy train line at 2,258 m.

The heart of it is a statue of Maitreya, the future Buddha, about 15 ft (4.6 m) tall, the Buddha who Buddhists believe is yet to come. Around him are old murals, butter lamps and shelves of scriptures wrapped in cloth. The monastery is modest in size and quiet most of the day; morning prayers, when the monks chant and the drums sound, are the best time to come. There is a small entry fee or a donation box, and photography inside the shrine hall may not be allowed, so ask first.

Most visitors arrive on the dawn Tiger Hill tour, along with Batasia Loop, which means a crowd between about 7 and 9 am in season. If you want peace, come later in the morning by shared jeep (₹30–50 from Darjeeling) or on the toy train joyride, which stops at Ghum station.

sections.heading: Samten Choling and the Sakya monastery
paras: Ghoom has two more monasteries that most tours skip. Samten Choling stands in Ghoom, a short walk from Yiga Choeling. The Sakya monastery, of the Sakya school, lies on the Hill Cart Road just below Ghoom on the Sonada side. We do not give founding dates for either here, because the figures we have seen do not agree.

Visiting all three on foot takes about two hours with time to sit. Follow the road and ask for directions; everyone in Ghoom knows them. Entry is free or by donation. If a puja is in progress, stand or sit quietly at the back and wait, rather than walking across the hall.

sections.heading: Bhutia Busty, Mahakal and the refugee centre
paras: Bhutia Busty monastery lies below Chowrasta on the slope toward the north, about 20–30 minutes on foot down a steep lane. The local account is that the monastery first stood on Observatory Hill and moved to its present site after damage in the Gorkha wars of the early 1800s; we repeat that as the story told locally rather than settled history. On clear days the mountains show across the valley from the slope around it.

Mahakal temple crowns Observatory Hill itself, a short steep climb from Chowrasta. It is one of the few places where Hindu and Buddhist priests share a shrine: Hindus worship Shiva as Mahakal, and Buddhists honour the same site, the old Dorje-ling of the town's name. Prayer flags and temple bells hang side by side. Watch out for monkeys; they snatch food and bags.

The Tibetan Refugee Self Help Centre, set up in October 1959 at Hill Side on the Lebong road, is not a monastery but belongs on this circuit. Refugee families started it to earn a living, and visitors can still walk through the workshops and watch carpets being woven on upright looms. There is a shop, and there is no pressure to buy.

sections.heading: Monasteries and shrines at a glance
paras: Distances are rounded from Chowrasta, and fees are indicative for 2025–26. Timings change with the season and the monastery calendar, so check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: A morning route that links them all
paras: You can see every site in this guide in a day and a half without a car. Take an early shared jeep from the Darjeeling stand to Ghoom, about ₹30–50 and 25–30 minutes, and reach Yiga Choeling for morning prayers. Walk on to Samten Choling and down to the Sakya monastery, then return to the road for tea and momos in Ghoom bazaar, where a plate costs about ₹80–150. If you have the energy, walk back down toward Darjeeling along the toy train line and stop at the Batasia Loop on the way; otherwise catch a jeep.

Spend the afternoon in town. Climb Observatory Hill to the Mahakal shrine, then follow the lanes down to Bhutia Busty while the light is still good. Keep the Tibetan Refugee Self Help Centre for the next weekday morning, when the looms are working, and combine it with Happy Valley Tea Estate, a short walk further down the Lebong road. Wear shoes you can slip off easily, carry small notes for donations and a warm layer for Ghoom, and you will spend very little beyond your jeep fares.

sections.heading: Etiquette inside a monastery
paras: Monks and caretakers are used to visitors and are usually welcoming. A few habits show respect and make the visit easier for everyone.
list: Walk clockwise around stupas, prayer wheels and the inside of shrine halls, and turn prayer wheels clockwise too.
Take off your shoes before entering a shrine hall if others have, and do not step on the raised threshold.
Dress modestly: shoulders and knees covered, hats off inside.
Ask before taking photographs, and never use a flash; many halls ban cameras inside.
Do not point your feet at the altar or at a monk when you sit, and do not sit on raised seats meant for lamas.
Do not touch statues, offerings or the scriptures on the shelves.
Keep your voice low during prayers and switch your phone to silent.
Put donations in the box or hand them over with both hands; ₹20–100 is a kind gesture.

sections.heading: Losar and festival days
paras: Losar, the Tibetan New Year, falls in February or March, following the lunar calendar. It is the time when the monasteries of Ghoom and Darjeeling are at their busiest: new prayer flags go up, families visit in their best clothes, and some monasteries hold prayers and masked dances in the days around it. Dates move each year, so check current status before you travel. Winter is cold at Ghoom, around 2,258 m, so bring warm layers if you come for Losar.

Other good days to visit are full-moon days, which carry special prayers, and Buddha Purnima in spring. On any morning, though, you can sit at the back of the hall, listen to the chanting and drink the butter tea if it is offered, which is often the visit people remember most.

faqs.q: Which is the most famous monastery in Darjeeling?
faqs.a: Yiga Choeling at Ghoom, usually called Ghoom Monastery, is the best known. It was founded in 1850 by Lama Sherab Gyatso, belongs to the Gelug school and houses a statue of Maitreya, the future Buddha, about 15 ft (4.6 m) tall. It is about 7–8 km from Darjeeling and is often visited on the dawn Tiger Hill tour.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee for Ghoom Monastery?
faqs.a: There is a small entry fee or donation at Yiga Choeling, and a further charge may apply for cameras. Samten Choling and the Sakya monastery nearby are free or by donation. Fees change, so check current status before you travel, and carry small notes. Photography inside the shrine hall may not be allowed, so always ask before taking pictures.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit monasteries in Darjeeling?
faqs.a: Early morning, when monks chant and the halls are quiet. Yiga Choeling gets busy between about 7 and 9 am in season, when Tiger Hill tour jeeps arrive, so later in the morning can be calmer. For the season, October to early December and March to April give clear skies. Losar, in February or March, is the most festive time.

faqs.q: How do I get to Ghoom Monastery from Darjeeling?
faqs.a: Take a shared jeep from Darjeeling to Ghoom for about ₹30–50 a seat, then walk a few minutes down from the main road. The toy train joyride also stops at Ghum station for about half an hour. A reserved car on the Tiger Hill dawn tour, about ₹1,500–2,200 a car, includes the monastery and Batasia Loop.

faqs.q: Why is the Mahakal temple shared by Hindus and Buddhists?
faqs.a: The temple on Observatory Hill stands where tradition places Dorje-ling, an old Buddhist shrine that may have given Darjeeling its name. Hindus worship Shiva there as Mahakal, and Buddhists honour the same site, so priests of both faiths serve the shrine side by side. It is a short steep climb from Chowrasta, best in the early morning. Beware of monkeys.

faqs.q: Can I take photos inside Darjeeling's monasteries?
faqs.a: Usually you can photograph the outside, the courtyards and the prayer wheels freely, but many shrine halls do not allow photography inside, and some charge a camera fee. Always ask a monk or caretaker first, never use a flash, and do not photograph people at prayer without permission. When in doubt, put the camera away and simply watch.

faqs.q: What should I wear to visit a monastery?
faqs.a: Wear clothes that cover your shoulders and knees, and take off hats inside. Shoes come off before entering a shrine hall if you see others leaving theirs at the door, so slip-on shoes help. Carry a warm layer, especially at Ghoom, which at about 2,258 m is cooler than Darjeeling and chilly in the mornings for most of the year.

faqs.q: Can visitors see the Tibetan Refugee Self Help Centre?
faqs.a: Yes. The centre, set up in October 1959 at Hill Side on the Lebong road, welcomes visitors to walk through its workshops and watch carpets being woven on upright looms. Entry is free, and there is a shop selling carpets and crafts. It is roughly a 30–40 minute walk from Chowrasta. Weekday working hours are the best time to see the looms busy.

faqs.q: When is Losar celebrated at Ghoom?
faqs.a: Losar, the Tibetan New Year, falls in February or March according to the lunar calendar, so the date moves each year. Around it, the Ghoom monasteries hold special prayers, families visit in new clothes and fresh prayer flags go up; some years include masked dances. Check current status before you travel, and pack warm clothes, since Ghoom is cold in late winter.
